work.title: Kleine Lieder für Kinder zur Beförderung der Tugend. Zweyter Theil

history.p: The second part of the collection including 30 children’s songs appeared in 1768 – that is, two years after the first part (SchW B5:Coll.002). Also this part was dedicated to the poet’s wife, Christiane Elisabeth Weiße. Apparently her husband Christian Felix had been approached by Scheibe sometime during summer 1765 who asked him whether he would send some moral or educational poems specifically written for children. According to Scheibe’s introduction to the first part of the collection, he and his publishers Korte in Flensburg had talked about remedying the lack of children’s songs. It was around the same time that Weiße had become a father, and having heard the tasteless songs sung by the wet nurse and child-carer he was inspired by the idea of writing a collection of new poems for children. When Scheibe had completed the first part, he continued with the second part. Meanwhile, Weiße published the poems in a revised version as Lieder für Kinder also adding new ones to the collection. Weiße’s poems were published again in 1768 (including an appendix) and again in 1770. To the second part, Scheibe added a new introduction which opens with a sharp response to a critique appearing in the journal Unterhaltungen (Hamburg, 1766). His response is extensive and deals with composing and with melodic and rhythmic structures; Scheibe refers to Friedrich Wilhelm Marpurg’s as well Johann Joseph Fux’s treatises and composers such as Johann Adolph Hasse, Georg Philipp Telemann and Carl Heinrich Graun. However, the second volume was already reviewed soon after its publication. Unterhaltungen has a long and detailed but anonymous critique and also includes numerous music examples responding to Scheibe's introduction. There is no doubt that the poems created an interest among intellectuals and educators, and the collection was reviewed in several German as well as Danish journals already in 1768. One of the songs of part two, ‘Der Mond’ (SchW B5:142), was reproduced in a review in Wöchentliche Nachrichten (1768) by the composer Johann Adam Hiller, and in 1769 he decided to use the same texts and published his Lieder für Kinder. Mit neuen Melodien. These were reviewed by Gerstenberg in Hamburgische Neue Zeitung (1769) who notes that 'a part of these songs were already composed in a larger form and indeed by a man who has undisputed merits regarding German music, among which the composition of his children's songs cannot be included.' Hiller’s melodies are light, simple and natural. In 1775, Hiller issued second edition, and now Scheibe is mentioned specifically: 'Contemporary songs have already been composed in a larger form by Mr. Kapellmeister in Copenhagen, and I was requested to present them on a smaller scale. To carry out this demand – and not to compare myself with another – I have composed new settings [of the poems].'
